title: JESUS SAID THE FIRST WILL BE LAST… SO WHY ARE CHRISTIANS FIGHTING SO HARD TO BE FIRST?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID THE FIRST WILL BE LAST… SO WHY ARE CHRISTIANS FIGHTING SO HARD TO BE FIRST?

We call it serving God. We call it leadership. We call it building His Kingdom. But what if some of the things we're fighting hardest to achieve are the very things Jesus warned us could destroy our hearts?
There is something deeply unsettling about watching Christians fight for the highest seat in a Kingdom whose King willingly took the lowest place.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that we have become so accustomed to it that we barely recognize the contradiction anymore.

We compete for positions. We compare ministries. We count followers. We celebrate titles. We measure influence. We quietly resent someone else's success while publicly congratulating them with a Bible verse.
We say, "To God be the glory."
But sometimes, buried beneath those beautiful words, there is another prayer we would never dare speak aloud.
"Lord, please make sure they notice me too."
And before you assume this article is about a particular pastor, church leader, Christian influencer, or someone who hurt you, I want you to consider something much more uncomfortable.
What if Jesus is speaking about you?
What if He is speaking about me?

What if the greatest danger to our spiritual lives is not that we have stopped believing in Jesus, but that we have learned to use His name while quietly pursuing the very greatness He taught us to surrender?
Because there is a moment in Scripture when Jesus said something that should make every ambitious Christian examine the motives behind their ambition.
"But many that are first shall be last; and the last shall be first." — Matthew 19:30, KJV
We have quoted those words for generations.
But have we actually allowed them to confront us?
Because Jesus was not merely giving humanity an inspirational lesson about humility.
He was overturning our assumptions about greatness, reward, privilege, and who truly belongs at the center of God's Kingdom.
And the closer we examine the conversation surrounding those words, the harder it becomes to hide behind religious appearances.
A wealthy young man had approached Jesus with a question about eternal life.
He appeared morally serious. He had kept the commandments he mentioned. He possessed the kind of outward respectability many religious communities would admire.
Yet Jesus exposed the one attachment he was unwilling to surrender.
His possessions.
Jesus told him to sell what he had, give to the poor, and follow Him (Matthew 19:16–22).
The young man walked away sorrowful.
Not because Jesus had nothing to offer him.
But because following Jesus would cost him something he was not prepared to release.
And here is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Not everyone walks away from Jesus because of money.
Some people cannot release their reputation.
Some cannot release their position.
Some cannot release their need to be admired.
Some cannot release the desire to be right, recognized, celebrated, or consulted.
Some would surrender their bank account before surrendering their title.
Others would sacrifice years of service before admitting that someone else might be more gifted than they are.
We can be physically present in the church while inwardly resisting the very Lord we claim to follow.
And that is a terrifying possibility.
After the wealthy man departed, Peter asked Jesus a question that sounds remarkably familiar.
"Behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee; what shall we have therefore?" (Matthew 19:27, KJV).
Peter was not wrong to ask about reward. Jesus did not rebuke him for asking, and He promised that the sacrifices of His followers would not be forgotten.
But Jesus also warned that many who were first would be last, and many who were last would be first.
Then, in Matthew 20, He told the parable of the laborers in the vineyard.
Some worked all day.
Others were hired later.
Yet the landowner paid them the same agreed daily wage.
Those who worked longest became angry, not because they had been cheated, but because others had received generosity they believed should have been reserved for people like themselves.
The landowner asked:
"Is thine eye evil, because I am good?" (Matthew 20:15, KJV).
That question still reaches into the hidden corners of religious hearts.
Can you rejoice when God is generous to someone who has served for fewer years than you?
Can you celebrate a new believer being welcomed into meaningful service without feeling that your decades of faithfulness have been diminished?
Can you watch God use someone else without quietly asking why He did not choose you?
Can you remain faithful when your labor is unseen and someone else's receives applause?
These are not small questions.
They expose whether we love the goodness of God or merely the benefits we hope His goodness will bring us.
And here is something we must understand about the original language.
In Matthew 19:30, the Greek text reads:
Πολλοὶ δὲ ἔσονται πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι.
Polloi de esontai prōtoi eschatoi kai eschatoi prōtoi.
A faithful rendering is:
"But many who are first will be last, and the last first."
The Greek word πρῶτοι (prōtoi) means "first" or "foremost."
The word ἔσχατοι (eschatoi) means "last."
These are words of position and order.
Jesus deliberately placed them in startling reversal.
But we must not twist His words into something He never intended.
He was not teaching that every successful person is wicked, that every unknown person is righteous, or that Christians should intentionally pursue failure.
Nor was He promising that every person who receives little recognition on earth will automatically receive the highest reward in heaven.
In context, Jesus was warning against human assumptions about status, entitlement, and reward in God's Kingdom.
God's generosity is not controlled by our comparisons.
His judgment is not governed by our popularity.
His grace cannot be purchased through seniority, visibility, or religious achievement.
And our place before Him is not secured by being more impressive than someone else.
That should humble every one of us.
Especially those who have spent years doing things in His name.
Because there is a kind of spiritual pride that does not look proud at first.
It looks hardworking.
It looks committed.
It looks disciplined.
It looks like someone who never misses a church activity.
It looks like someone who knows exactly how to speak, pray, teach, and behave in public.
But beneath all that activity, the heart can slowly begin asking a dangerous question.
"After everything I've done for God, shouldn't I be more important by now?"
And once that question takes root, service can become competition.
Ministry can become territory.
Leadership can become ownership.
And the people we were called to love can become obstacles to the recognition we believe we deserve.
Perhaps you have seen it.
A gifted young believer begins serving, and instead of being discipled, they are treated as a threat.
A church member receives an opportunity, and another quietly withdraws because they were not chosen.
A pastor rejoices publicly over another ministry's growth but privately feels diminished by it.
A Christian posts Scripture online, then becomes discouraged because a message about Jesus receives fewer reactions than a photograph of someone else's lifestyle.
Or perhaps you have lived on the other side.
You served faithfully for years.
You stayed when others left.
You cleaned rooms no one noticed.
You gave when money was tight.
You prayed for people who never knew your name.
And when an opportunity finally appeared, someone newer was chosen.
You smiled.
You said you understood.
You even told them you were happy for them.
But later, alone, you wondered whether God had forgotten you.
If that is your story, please hear this carefully.
Being overlooked by people does not mean you have been overlooked by God.
But neither does being overlooked automatically make you spiritually superior.
That distinction matters.
Because even our wounds can become another place where pride quietly grows.
We can begin believing that because others failed to appreciate us, God must consider us better than them.
And suddenly, the person who once wanted the highest seat begins taking pride in being the most misunderstood person in the room.
The heart is capable of turning almost anything into a competition.
Even suffering.
Even sacrifice.
Even humility.
That is why we need more than a lesson in better behavior.
We need Jesus to search us.
And perhaps no scene exposes the tragedy of religious ambition more clearly than what happened immediately after Jesus warned about the first and the last.
In Matthew 20:17–19, Jesus told His disciples that He was going to Jerusalem, where He would be condemned, mocked, scourged, crucified, and raised on the third day.
Think about the weight of that moment.
The Son of God was speaking about His approaching suffering.
He was describing the road to the cross.
He was preparing His followers for the darkest hours they would witness.
And shortly afterward, the mother of James and John approached Him with her sons and requested that they receive the seats at His right and left in His Kingdom (Matthew 20:20–21).
Jesus was speaking about suffering.
They were thinking about seats.
Jesus was moving toward humiliation.
They were imagining promotion.
Jesus was preparing to give His life.
They were asking for places of honor.
And before we condemn them too quickly, we should recognize how easily we do the same thing.
We stand beneath the symbol of a crucified Savior while fighting over who gets to stand closest to the spotlight.
We sing about surrender while protecting our influence.
We preach about dying to self while becoming offended when our preferences are not followed.
We speak of unity while quietly building circles of loyalty around ourselves.
And sometimes the greatest scandal is not what the world says about the church.
It is how little our ambitions resemble the Christ we proclaim.
The other ten disciples became indignant with the two brothers.
But Jesus did not resolve the conflict by choosing a winner.
He called them together and redefined greatness itself.
"Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister; And whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant." (Matthew 20:26–27, KJV).
In the Greek, the word translated "minister" is διάκονος (diakonos), meaning a servant or one who serves.
The word translated "servant" in verse 27 is δοῦλος (doulos), a word commonly meaning slave or bondservant.
The language becomes progressively more demanding.
Jesus was not offering a clever strategy for becoming famous through humility.
He was telling His disciples that greatness in His Kingdom must be understood through service rather than domination.
Then He gave the reason.
"Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." (Matthew 20:28, KJV).
There it is.
The center of the entire conversation.
Jesus Himself.
Not a leadership technique.
Not a formula for church growth.
Not a strategy for becoming influential.
A Savior who gave His life.
The Greek word translated "ransom" is λύτρον (lytron), referring to the price of release or redemption.
Jesus did not merely come to teach people how to become kinder.
He came to give His life for sinners.
His service led to the cross.
And the cross exposes the emptiness of every attempt to turn Christianity into a contest for personal glory.
Consider what this means.
The One who possessed all authority did not need to prove His importance through human applause.
The One worthy of worship knelt to wash His disciples' feet (John 13:1–17).
The One who could command angels submitted to suffering.
The One without sin bore the consequences of sin for others.
And the One who was truly first willingly entered the place of shame and rejection to accomplish our redemption.
Philippians 2:5–8 calls believers to have the mind of Christ, who humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
But the passage does not end in humiliation.
God highly exalted Him (Philippians 2:9–11).
This is essential.
Jesus was not a defeated servant trying to earn importance.
He is the eternal Son, whose humility revealed the character of His saving mission.
His exaltation is not a reward for cleverly making Himself look small.
It is the Father's vindication of the crucified and risen Lord.
And our calling is not to imitate His unique work of redemption, which only He could accomplish, but to follow His example of humble, sacrificial love.
That changes everything.
Because the Christian life is not a race to prove that we deserve to be first.
It is a life of grace in which we learn to love because Christ first loved us.
And perhaps you need to hear something else.
You do not have to become impressive to become precious to God.
The gospel does not begin with your accomplishments.
It begins with your need.
It begins with the truth that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23).
It continues with the astonishing announcement that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8).
And it calls us to repentance and faith in the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
We are not saved by being the most generous, the most gifted, the most admired, or the most active person in church.
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV).
Yet the very next verse tells us that we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
Grace does not make service unnecessary.
Grace makes service something different.
We no longer serve to purchase God's acceptance.
We serve because, in Christ, we have received mercy we could never earn.
And when that truth settles into the heart, something beautiful begins to happen.
You can serve without demanding recognition.
You can lead without needing to control everyone.
You can give without announcing the amount.
You can celebrate another believer's calling without feeling threatened by it.
You can apologize without protecting your image.
You can admit that someone younger knows something you need to learn.
You can step aside when wisdom requires it.
You can remain faithful when no one applauds.
Not because your feelings never get hurt.
Not because you never struggle with envy.
But because the approval of Christ begins to matter more than the applause of people.
And there is another moment in Scripture that makes this painfully vivid.
On the night Jesus was betrayed, the disciples were still arguing about greatness.
Luke 22:24 records that there was strife among them over which should be accounted the greatest.
Think about that.
The cross was approaching.
Judas's betrayal was unfolding.
Jesus was preparing to suffer.
And His closest followers were still concerned with rank.
If even the apostles struggled with this, why would we imagine ourselves immune?
Jesus told them:
"I am among you as he that serveth." (Luke 22:27, KJV).
What an astonishing sentence.
The Lord of glory stood among men who were arguing about importance and identified Himself as the One who serves.
He did not deny His authority.
He demonstrated what godly authority looks like.
And this should challenge every Christian who leads a ministry, manages a team, raises a family, teaches Scripture, or holds influence over others.
Authority is not permission to make people feel small.
Leadership is not a license to demand unquestioning admiration.
Spiritual maturity is not measured by how many people depend on you.
And being entrusted with responsibility never places someone beyond correction.
Jesus warned against rulers who exercise domination over others.
He called His followers to a different way.
Not the absence of responsibility.
Not the rejection of all leadership.
But leadership transformed by love, accountability, humility, and service.
A church does not become more Christlike simply because its leaders become more famous.
A ministry does not become more faithful simply because its audience grows.
A Christian does not become more holy simply because a platform becomes larger.
Growth can be a blessing.
Influence can be stewarded faithfully.
Recognition can open doors for the gospel.
But none of those things is reliable proof of spiritual maturity.
The question is not merely how many people know your name.
It is whether the people who encounter your life are being pointed toward Jesus.
And here is where this message becomes even more personal.
Imagine a church gathering where no one knows who donated the most.
No one is competing for the microphone.
No one is offended because someone else was asked to pray.
No one treats new believers as inferior.
No one mistakes quietness for insignificance.
The elderly widow is honored.
The struggling young father is encouraged.
The recovering sinner is discipled rather than endlessly reminded of their past.
The person who cleans the floor is treated with the same dignity as the person who preaches from the pulpit.
And when someone falls into sin, the church does not celebrate their humiliation.
It pursues truth, accountability, repentance, protection for those harmed, and restoration where biblically appropriate.
Wouldn't that look more like the Kingdom Jesus described?
Of course, no earthly congregation will embody these things perfectly.
We are still people being sanctified.
But that is precisely why the call to humility matters.
Because the church is not a museum of people who have successfully become first.
It is a community of sinners saved by grace, learning to follow the One who gave Himself for them.
And if you have been wounded by pride inside the church, I want to speak to you for a moment.
Perhaps someone treated you as unimportant because you had no title.
Perhaps your contributions were forgotten.
Perhaps you were made to feel that your value depended on how much money you gave, how visible your service was, or how useful you were to someone's ministry.
That was not a faithful reflection of the heart of Jesus.
You are not less worthy of dignity because you cannot afford a large offering.
You are not spiritually inferior because you do not have a public platform.
You are not invisible to God because people have forgotten your sacrifices.
Hebrews 6:10 reminds believers that God is not unrighteous to forget their work and labor of love shown toward His name.
And if you have been the person who overlooked others, dismissed their pain, demanded recognition, or treated ministry as personal property, there is still a way home.
It begins with repentance.
Not excuses.
Not a carefully worded public statement designed to preserve your reputation.
Not blaming the people who confronted you.
Repentance.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, involving a change of mind and a turning away from sin.
Biblical repentance is more than embarrassment over being exposed.
It is a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Sometimes that means confessing a hidden motive.
Sometimes it means asking forgiveness from someone you mistreated.
Sometimes it means making restitution.
Sometimes it means surrendering a position you have used selfishly.
Sometimes it means accepting correction without treating the person who corrected you as an enemy.
And sometimes it begins with a prayer so simple that pride has spent years preventing you from saying it.
"Jesus, I wanted people to see me more than I wanted them to see You. Forgive me."
There is no shame in bringing that confession to the Savior who already knows your heart.
There is danger in refusing to bring it.
Because the greatest tragedy is not discovering pride within yourself.
The greater tragedy is defending it until you can no longer recognize it.
Remember Peter?
The same disciple who asked what reward the apostles would receive later denied Jesus three times.
The man who had confidently declared his loyalty collapsed under fear.
And after the resurrection, Jesus restored him through a searching conversation about love and a renewed call to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Jesus did not pretend Peter's failure had never happened.
Nor did He treat Peter's failure as the final word over his life.
He called him back to love and service.
"Feed my sheep."
Not "Build your reputation."
Not "Make everyone acknowledge your importance."
Not "Prove you are greater than the other disciples."
Care for the people who belong to Me.
And then, when Peter turned and asked about John's future, Jesus redirected him.
"What is that to thee? follow thou me." (John 21:22, KJV).
What a devastatingly beautiful answer to the disease of comparison.
Peter, stop measuring your calling against someone else's.
That is still the invitation.
You do not need another person's assignment.
You do not need another person's audience.
You do not need another person's position.
You need to be faithful to the Lord who called you.
And if He has entrusted you with much, steward it humbly.
If He has entrusted you with something hidden, serve faithfully.
If He has called you to lead, lead as one accountable to Christ.
If He has called you to support another person's ministry, do so without imagining that support makes you less important.
Because in the Kingdom of God, faithfulness is not made worthless by obscurity.
And visibility does not automatically equal faithfulness.
There is one more thing we need to confront.
We can even turn Christian generosity into another competition.
But Scripture will not allow us to manipulate consciences that way.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
The Greek word ἀνάγκης (anankēs), translated "necessity" in this verse, conveys constraint or compulsion.
Giving should not be extracted through pressure.
Supporting gospel work can be a beautiful act of generosity and stewardship.
Philippians 4:15–18 shows believers materially supporting Paul's ministry, and Paul describes their gift in language of worship pleasing to God.
But such support must remain voluntary, honest, and directed toward faithful work.
This matters deeply to us at Gospel Warrior.
That would contradict the very gospel we are trying to proclaim.
Instead, we want to invite you into something meaningful.
It is one way you can give toward gospel-centered work alongside your other responsibilities and commitments, including the support you give to your local church.
We do not want your giving to come from fear.
We want it to come from love.
But even more important than a discount is the purpose behind the ministry.
We want to keep opening Scripture.
Keep confronting comfortable lies.
Keep encouraging wounded believers.
Keep calling sinners to repentance and faith.
Keep reminding the discouraged that their story does not have to end where their failure began.
And keep pointing people to Jesus Christ, because only He saves.
Your worth before God is not determined by your ability to pay.
You can still help this message reach someone who needs it.
Not because sharing makes you spiritually superior.

But because somewhere in your circle of friends may be a believer who is exhausted from trying to be noticed, a church leader who needs a gentle but serious confrontation, or someone who has walked away from Christian community after being wounded by religious pride.
One thoughtful share may open a conversation you never expected.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something.
Not as a demand.
Not as a performance.
As an invitation to spiritual honesty.
When you look at your own life, where has the desire to be first begun competing with your desire to follow Christ?
Is it in your church?
Your ministry?
Your family?
Your career?
Your online presence?
Or in that quiet place inside your heart where you keep wondering why God seems to be blessing everyone else?
Or share what God is teaching you about humility, comparison, and surrender.
You do not need to reveal private wounds or confess sensitive matters publicly. But your sincere testimony may encourage someone else who is wrestling with the same struggle.
Because there are people reading this who have spent years believing that if they could just become more visible, more successful, more respected, more accomplished, they would finally feel secure.
And perhaps the Holy Spirit is bringing them back to a much simpler truth.
Christ is enough.
Not because ambition is always sinful.
Not because hard work is wrong.
Not because excellence should be abandoned.
But because no earthly achievement can carry the weight of being your savior.
Jesus never commanded His disciples to become careless, passive, or unfaithful.
He called them to follow Him.
To love one another.
To bear fruit.
To make disciples.
To remain faithful.
And to remember that the greatest among them must be a servant.
So pursue excellence, but refuse to worship recognition.
Accept responsibility, but never confuse authority with superiority.
Work diligently, but do not turn another person's success into evidence of your failure.
Give generously, but never imagine you can purchase God's favor.
Serve faithfully, but remember that even your best works cannot replace the grace of Christ.
And when pride rises again, because it will, return to the cross.
Look at the Savior who was mocked while accomplishing our redemption.
Look at the hands that washed feet and were later pierced.
Look at the King who wore a crown of thorns before being revealed in resurrection glory.
Look at the empty tomb.
And remember whose Kingdom this is.
It is not yours.
It is not mine.
It belongs to Jesus.
One day, the applause of this world will fall silent.
The titles we fought to acquire will no longer impress anyone.
The follower counts will not determine our standing before God.
The positions we guarded so fiercely will be left behind.
And what will matter is not whether we succeeded in making ourselves the center of the story.
What matters eternally is whether we belong to Christ, the Savior who died and rose again, and whether our lives bear witness to His transforming grace.
So perhaps the prayer we need tonight is not:
"Lord, make me first."
Perhaps it is:
"Lord, make me faithful."
"Teach me to love people I once considered competition."
"Teach me to celebrate what You are doing in someone else's life."
"Forgive me for using holy things to feed an unholy desire for recognition."
"Free me from the exhausting need to prove my importance."
"Make me willing to serve when nobody is watching."
"And when people encounter my life, let them see more of Jesus and less of my pride."
Because this is what grace does.
It does not merely forgive our scandals.
It begins transforming the hearts that created them.
It takes the disciple who wanted the highest seat and teaches him to care for sheep.
It takes the believer who wanted applause and teaches her the beauty of unseen faithfulness.
It takes the wounded servant who thought being overlooked meant being worthless and reminds that servant of God's enduring love.
It takes people like you and me, proud, insecure, ambitious, frightened, and sometimes terribly confused about what greatness means, and calls us back to the feet of Jesus.
There is room for repentance.
There is mercy for the proud who turn to Christ.
There is forgiveness for those who have misused influence.
There is hope for those who have been crushed by comparison.
And there is a better way to live.
Not by fighting harder to be first.
But by following more closely the One who is Lord of all.
Because the saddest thing would be to spend your whole life fighting for the highest seat, only to realize you were too busy seeking a throne to notice the Savior kneeling with a towel.
